extracted.intended_audience: student reporters / newspaper journalists learning to write news stories of speeches, interviews, and reports
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporters on writing news stories that reproduce speeches, interviews, addresses, lectures, sermons, and written reports — focusing on accuracy, treatment (condensing/summarizing), human-interest handling, and avoidance of distortion or bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification: speeches, interviews, and reports as utterances
rubrics_metrics.description: Speeches, lectures, addresses, and sermons may be considered in the same class with interviews and reports, because all are alike in being some form of utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A speech differs from a report only in that one is spoken and the other written; an interview may be regarded as an informal address delivered to an audience of one. When an interview is given in question-and-answer form, it resembles cross-examination in a court story more than a speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose: accurate reproduction of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: To reproduce as accurately as possible the ideas expressed by a speaker, by a person interviewed, or by the author of a report is the only object in writing a news story dealing with such material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All quotation, direct or indirect, should be accurate not only in substance and form but also in spirit. A statement taken verbatim may be played up in the lead in such a way that it does not give the actual thought or purpose of the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in recording: avoid carelessness
rubrics_metrics.description: Carelessness in taking down what is said endangers the accuracy of news stories of this type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters must take careful notes or stenographic copies; in some events verbatim copies may be supplied (example: a stenographer's verbatim taken of President Wilson's speech to be sent to newspapers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual integrity: avoid misleading extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't play up statements taken from their context in a way that is misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confined selection of only one or two phases of a speech can give an erroneous impression of the whole. Leads or emphasis that distort the original thought or purpose are unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid distortion and partisan misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distortion and suppression of speeches, interviews, or reports because of political or other bias is indefensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misrepresentation because of political partisanship or other bias must be avoided; news organizations (e.g., Associated Press) aim to furnish world news 'untainted and without bias of any sort.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations must be accurate in substance, form, and spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: All quotation, direct or indirect, should be accurate not only in substance and form but also in spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A verbatim statement may still mislead if taken out of context or emphasized improperly; accuracy includes preserving intended meaning and emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment: condense, summarize, and unify
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief problem is condensing, summarizing, and combining different parts of the available material into a unified, coherent whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because stories of this class consist largely of direct and indirect quotation, the reporter must skillfully select and compress material so the story reads as a coherent piece rather than a disconnected series of excerpts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest development (especially in interviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews offer a chance to bring out human interest by portraying the character and personality of the person interviewed; speeches and reports offer little field for human-interest development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use description of the speaker and circumstances when appropriate to stimulate reader interest; this is less available for straightforward reports or sermons but valuable in feature-style interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling reporter questions in interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporter's questions, which are a necessary means of obtaining expression of ideas, are often suppressed in many stories; sometimes questions are embodied in the answers or are repeated by the person interviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a growing tendency, particularly in signed interview stories, to give the reporter's questions. Decide whether including the Qs improves clarity/honesty of the exchange or whether suppressing them produces a smoother narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of descriptive detail sparingly to interest readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Except for occasional opportunity to describe the speaker or the audience, news stories of speeches and reports must be largely informative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visual or atmospheric details (speaker gestures, audience reaction, setting) to stimulate reader interest, but do not let description overshadow accurate reporting of the utterance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format choice affects tone: Q&A vs narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: An interview in Q&A form resembles cross-examination and reads differently than a narrative reproduction of a speech; format choice should suit the material and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the direct Q&A will serve the story's 목적 (e.g., court-story feel) or whether a summarized narrative will better convey the speaker's ideas and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial restraint: avoid giving disproportionate emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Unintentional distortion can result from giving disproportionate space or emphasis to some points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reporters should balance space allocation so that no small point is magnified to the detriment of the true scope of the speech or report.
